label: prf:sw-period-residue-sum
title: Proof that the Seiberg–Witten period is an algebraic residue sum
html:
By the MI--SW abelianisation, the n-th prolonged Seiberg--Witten differential \lambda_{\mathrm{SW}}^{(n)} is the Cartan component of the abelianised connection on the exceptional divisor \mathcal{S}_c \cong \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}). As a connection 1-form on a genus-zero curve it is meromorphic, with poles confined to the branch points z_c (the only points where the prolonged connection degenerates).

\mathcal{S}_c is compact, so \lambda_{\mathrm{SW}}^{(n)} has finitely many poles p_1,\dots,p_k, all at branch points. For a cycle \gamma bounding a region whose poles are E \subseteq \{p_1,\dots,p_k\}, the residue theorem gives

\oint_{\gamma}\lambda_{\mathrm{SW}}^{(n)}
\;=\;
2\pi i \sum_{p_j\,\in\,E}\mathrm{Res}_{p_j}\,\lambda_{\mathrm{SW}}^{(n)},

the right-hand side being a finite sum of local residues. Identifying the left-hand side with the prolonged period a_D^{(n)} of Abelianisation of the MI integral on exceptional divisors gives the residue-sum shape: the period is computed by collecting residues, with no contour integration — once E is known.

Scope. The argument cannot run over all k poles, nor appeal to a period over a generating cycle of \mathcal{S}_c. \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}) has H_1 = 0, so there is no generating cycle; and the residue theorem on a compact Riemann surface states that the residues over all poles sum to zero, which would give a_D^{(n)} = 0 at every level rather than the positive binding period the keystone requires. This vanishing is a derived consequence rather than a claim, and its contrapositive — a nonzero period forces a nonzero total residue — is what forces E to be a proper subset. The companion statement The Seiberg–Witten period is an algebraic residue sum carries the residue-sum shape as an explicit hypothesis; it does not derive it. \qquad\blacksquare
